**What it gives up.** Simplicity, and the empty spaces the carries leave behind. A seam-flat defender
running up the field with #2 is not in the flat, so a quick out by #1, or the back releasing to the
flat, is open underneath him. And any route combination that makes two defenders' rules collide
becomes a target: [post-wheel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post-wheel) (the corner carries the
post inside while the wheel goes up the sideline behind the seam-flat defender), switch releases
that cross #1 and #2 at the snap, and motion that changes who is #2 at the last moment. The match
coverage's rules close the seams; offensive coaches now design plays to open the gaps between the
rules.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-verts-match
#| fig-cap: "The same four verticals against Cover 3 match (simulated, BDB-format tracking). Now the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS), the seam-flat defenders (ringed), read the slot receivers: both go vertical, so each walls his man and carries him up the seam, running underneath and inside him. The corners carry X and Z as before. The free safety (FS) no longer has two seams to himself; he sits in the middle over both carries, ready to help on either. Four vertical routes now face four defenders deep, plus a safety. The quarterback holds the ball and checks down to the back (R), who has released to the flat that the carries emptied; the Mike (M), matched to the back, has to run him down from the hook, about 5 yards away when the ball arrives, for a gain of four or five. On the web this is a video."
match = verts("match")
MATCH_T = [0.0, 1.0, 2.1, arrival(match, "RB", 2.6)]
if PDF:
    strip(match, MATCH_T,
          ["Snap · same shell", "+1.0 s · the walls", "+2.1 s · the carries", f"+{MATCH_T[3]:.1f} s · the check-down"],
          ["Same picture: 3 deep,\n4 under",
           "#2s go vertical: $ and\nSS wall them and run",
           "Each seam: a defender\nunder it, the FS over it",
           "Nothing deep: ball to R in\nthe flat; M runs him down"],
          LAT_V, WIN_V, rings=("NB", "SS"), throw_t=2.6)
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(match, times=MATCH_T)
```

Compare the second panels of the two plays. In spot-drop, the nickel and the strong safety ran away
from the slot receivers toward their curl landmarks. In match, they ran *with* them. That's the
whole difference, and it's visible on a broadcast replay if you watch the slot defender for one
second. Now each seam has a defender underneath it and the free safety above, a two-on-one in the
defense's favour on both sides, and the quarterback who expected one safety and two seams finds
nobody open. He checks the ball down to the back in the flat, the space the two carries emptied,
and the Mike has to run him down from the hook. Four or five yards: the price of carrying both seams,
and one the defense will pay every time instead of a 25-yard seam.

### What offenses attack instead

Match rules are a set of if-then statements, and an offense that knows them can write a route
combination in which every defender obeys his rule and the rules still leave a hole. The cleanest
example is the post-wheel.

```{python}
#| label: fig-post-wheel
#| fig-cap: "Post-wheel against Cover 3 match, on the offense's left. X (#1) starts vertical and breaks to the post at about 12 yards; by rule the corner (CB, ringed) carries a vertical #1 on top, so he goes inside with him. H (#2) runs toward the flat, so by rule the nickel ($, ringed) goes with him, underneath; then H turns up the sideline (the wheel). The corner is inside, the nickel is trailing from below, and the free safety (FS) is in the middle: the sideline behind them (green) is empty. Every defender obeyed his rule; together the rules left the hole."
PW_PRE = {"NB": (5.0, -7.0), "LCB": (7.5, -16.3), "FS": (14.5, 0.0), "WILL": (4.5, -2.2)}
PW_POST = {"NB": (11.0, -19.6), "LCB": (21.5, -11.4), "FS": (19.0, -3.4), "WILL": (9.0, -4.2)}
pw = Play(spread(), nickel(C3_POST | PW_POST), los=LOS, to_go=None)
pw.highlight("NB", "LCB")
fld = draw(pw, lateral=(-26.67, 7.4), window=(-7.5, 30.0), width_in=5.0)
route_line(fld, pw, [(-0.7, -15.0), (11.5, -15.6), (25.0, -9.8)], lw=1.7)
route_line(fld, pw, [(-1.5, -9.0), (1.4, -12.6), (3.6, -18.4), (8.6, -21.6), (25.5, -22.4)], lw=1.7)
for k in PW_PRE:
    ghost(fld, pw, *PW_PRE[k], LAB[k][1])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["LCB"], (13.5, -16.4), PW_POST["LCB"]])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["NB"], (3.6, -14.6), PW_POST["NB"]])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["FS"], PW_POST["FS"]])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["WILL"], PW_POST["WILL"]])
hole(fld, pw, 21.5, -22.0, 4.6, 6.0, "")
say(fld, pw, 26.8, -19.5, "wheel: open up\nthe sideline", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.4)
say(fld, pw, 15.4, -7.6, "#1 post: the CB\ncarries him inside", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
say(fld, pw, 6.6, -23.2, "#2 to the\nflat: $ goes\nwith him", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
for k, txt in (("X", "#1"), ("H", "#2")):
    q = pw.players[k]
    say(fld, pw, q.d - 2.4, q.w, txt, fontsize=6.2)
plt.show()
```

Two other answers don't need a picture once you see this one. A **switch release** crosses #1 and
#2 at the snap, the outside receiver running inside and the slot running outside, so the corner and
the seam-flat defender, each reading "his" number, have to decide in the first step who is now #1
and who is #2; if they hesitate or both take the same man, the other one is free. And **motion**
changes the count late: a slot who motions across the formation turns a 2x2 into trips, so the
defense's numbering, its rotation side and possibly its trips check all have to change in the
seconds before the snap. The defense's counter is communication, which is why match defenses talk
so much before every snap.

### The trips problem

Match rules work cleanly against 2x2, two receivers each side. Against
[3x1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1) (trips: three receivers to one side), Cover 3 has a
counting problem: four underneath defenders, but three receivers on one side whose routes can all go
vertical. If #3, the innermost trips receiver, runs straight up the middle, who carries him? In
spot-drop it's the free safety, and he can't be on #3 and over #2's seam at the same time, so the
trips side's seam falls to the corner and the curl-flat defender, who are guarding other things. Match
teams answer with a trips *check*, a pre-planned adjustment (the two-high versions are the
[3x1 checks](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1-check) of
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)). The
check doesn't add a defender; it moves one. In one common version the backside corner takes the
lone receiver on the other side by himself, man to man wherever he goes (Saban's playbook calls this
[MEG](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-meg), "man everywhere he goes"). That frees the defenders who
would have helped on the backside to slide toward the trips, where the trips-side corner and the free
safety stay the deep players and one of the freed underneath defenders (which one varies by staff)
takes #3 if he goes vertical, so the free safety can stay over #2. Saban's system names its trips
checks (one is "Mable," in which the safety comes down toward the trips), and every NFL staff has
its own.[^mable] The tell for a viewer: against trips, look at the backside corner. If he's pressing
the single receiver, alone, with no safety leaning his way, the defense has probably checked its
Cover 3 to put its help on the trips side.
([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) covers
the two-high answers to trips, including rotating to Cover 3 match.)

## Seattle's version: Cover 3 as an identity

For most of the 2000s, Cover 3 was something defenses played on early downs between the more
fashionable calls. Then Pete Carroll's Seattle Seahawks made it the most feared defense in football,
mostly by showing one pre-snap picture, a single high safety and corners pressed on the receivers,
and playing two coverages behind it: Cover 3 and its man twin, Cover 1 ("man free").[^durkin]
[Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) met this defense in its film room; here
is why it worked as a *scheme*.

Carroll had spent decades as a defensive backs coach, coordinator and head coach before Seattle hired
him in 2010; Gus Bradley ran the defense from 2009 to 2012 and Dan Quinn in 2013 and 2014.[^staff]
Carroll's idea, laid out in his book *Win Forever*, was that a program needs one clearly defined
philosophy and should try to do things "better than they have ever been done before."[^winforever]
On defense, that meant a 4-3 front with a one-high safety and five distinctive pieces:

1. **A free safety with rare range.** Earl Thomas, the 14th pick of the 2010 draft, covered the deep
   middle third alone, and fast enough to arrive at either seam. Cover 3 lives or dies with its post
   safety; Seattle's could erase mistakes in front of him.
2. **A strong safety built like a linebacker.** Kam Chancellor, a fifth-round pick that same year,
   was the eighth man in the box: the sky or buzz player who came down at the snap, the force or
   alley defender against the run, and a seam-flat defender who could carry a tight end up the
   field.
3. **Tall corners who pressed and carried.** Richard Sherman and Brandon Browner (both 6 feet 3 or
   taller, a fifth-round pick and a Canadian Football League signing)[^draft] lined up on receivers'
   noses, jammed them inside the 5-yard limit with Carroll's step-kick technique, and if the receiver
   went deep, ran *with* him into the corner's own deep third. That press looked exactly like man
   coverage, which is the point: before the snap the quarterback couldn't tell Cover 3 from Cover 1.
   The difference shows only after it, when a receiver breaks inside. In Cover 1 the corner follows
   him across the field; in Cover 3 he lets him go and sinks.
4. **Match rules on the verticals.** The corners carried #1's vertical release like man defenders,
   the down safety matched a seam route from his underneath spot, and the free safety leaned toward
   the other seam (the "both versions" note in the match section), so four verticals met four
   defenders.[^match]
5. **Repetition.** With few calls, the players practised the same reads thousands of times, and
   rarely blew an assignment. The scheme was simple enough to play fast.

The results were extraordinary. Seattle allowed the fewest points in the NFL four seasons running,
2012 to 2015, the first team to do so since the Cleveland Browns of the 1950s.[^points]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks, Super Bowl XLVIII (Feb. 2, 2014) — one buzz snap"}
Early in the third quarter, Seattle leading Denver 29–0. Denver lines up in 11 personnel with twins
to the right, Wes Welker in the slot; Kam Chancellor is on the other side, over the tight end. The
call is buzz: Chancellor's landing spot is the hook-curl on his side. Byron Maxwell, at corner,
starts pressed on the line.

At the snap the tight end and the receiver on Chancellor's side both run go routes. Chancellor, in
his own words, "stayed with the tight end up the seam, keeping one eye on Peyton in the backfield":
the seam carry, from the buzz spot, exactly as the match table says. Then Welker comes underneath
on a drag, into the zone Chancellor has just left. Chancellor can let the tight end go because Earl
Thomas is in the post over the top, so he peels off, drives on Welker, and punches the ball away: pass
broken up.[^xlviii]

**What to notice:** one defender doing three jobs in three seconds, in the order the chapter
taught: buzz down inside, carry the seam while it's a threat, come off it when the deep safety has
it and the ball goes underneath. That's Cover 3 match, and that's why Seattle needed a strong
safety who could run with a tight end and still hit like a linebacker.
:::

### The tree

Carroll's assistants took the scheme with them, and for a while Seattle-style Cover 3 was the
NFL's fastest-spreading defense. Bradley went on to coach or coordinate four more defenses
(Jacksonville, the Chargers, the Raiders and the Colts); Quinn took Atlanta to Super Bowl LI as head
coach and is Washington's head coach today.[^tree] Robert Saleh, a junior
[quality-control](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quality-control-coach) assistant in Seattle (the
entry-level staffer who breaks down film), built his first San Francisco defenses on the same
eight-man-front Cover 3 before mixing in more coverages.[^saleh] The tree is still growing: Saleh,
the Tennessee Titans' head coach in 2026, hired Bradley as his defensive coordinator.

You can follow the coaches through the data. Bradley is the clearest case, because he moved three
times in five years.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bradley
#| fig-cap: "Follow the coach: the share of each defense's charted dropbacks played in Cover 3, 2018–2022 (Next Gen Stats charting via nflverse). Orange points are seasons in which Gus Bradley, Seattle's defensive coordinator from 2009 to 2012, ran that defense; grey points are seasons he didn't. The dashed line is the league average (32 percent). Bradley's 2019 and 2018 Chargers and his 2021 Raiders posted the three highest Cover 3 rates of any defense in this period (his 2020 Chargers were sixth), and the Raiders' rate jumped from 18 to 65 percent the year he arrived and fell back to 27 percent the year he left."
C3_SHARE = COV.assign(c3=COV["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_3")).groupby(["defteam", "season"])["c3"].mean()
LEAGUE = COV["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_3").mean()
BRADLEY = {"LAC": ("Chargers", {2018, 2019, 2020}), "LV": ("Raiders", {2021}), "IND": ("Colts", {2022})}
seasons = list(range(2018, 2023))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.5), sharey=True)
for ax, (team, (name, years)) in zip(axes, BRADLEY.items()):
    vals = [C3_SHARE.get((team, s), np.nan) for s in seasons]
    ax.plot(seasons, vals, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    for s, v in zip(seasons, vals):
        on = s in years
        ax.scatter([s], [v], s=34 if on else 22, color=style.DEFENSE if on else GREY, zorder=3,
                   edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
        ax.text(s, v + 0.035, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.3,
                color=DD if on else style.INK_2)
    ax.axhline(LEAGUE, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=8, loc="left", color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xticks(seasons, [f"'{s % 100:02d}" for s in seasons], fontsize=7)
    ax.set_ylim(0.0, 0.9)
    ax.set_xlim(2017.55, 2022.45)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axes[0].tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Cover 3 share of dropbacks", fontsize=7.5)
axes[0].text(2018.0, LEAGUE - 0.07, "league average", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2)
handles = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.DEFENSE, ms=6, label="Bradley ran the defense"),
           Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=GREY, ms=5, label="another coordinator")]
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The pattern is hard to miss. The 2019 Chargers played Cover 3 on 74 percent of their charted
dropbacks, the highest rate of any defense from 2018 to 2022; the 2018 Chargers and the 2021 Raiders
were second and third. When Bradley left Los Angeles the Chargers fell to the league average; when he
arrived in Las Vegas the Raiders more than tripled their rate; when he left, it fell back. Coaches
are their schemes, and a coverage this simple travels well. Indianapolis is the weaker case, and
it's worth saying why. The Colts' rate rose from 29 to 41 percent in Bradley's first year, a real
jump but nothing like Las Vegas, partly because his predecessor, Matt Eberflus, had already played
Cover 3 above the league average in two of his four seasons (38 percent in 2018), and partly because by 2022 the whole league
was moving toward two-high shells.[^colts] (The chart stops in 2022 because this charting source
does.) (Not every member of the tree stayed
with it: Quinn's 2021 Cowboys played Cover 3 on about 27 percent of their dropbacks, below the
league average, part of a broader shift you'll see next.)

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Chargers 2019 and Las Vegas Raiders 2021 — the coverage in the numbers"}
If you want to see Seattle's Cover 3 without Seattle's players, Bradley's Chargers are the best
library: a single-high safety, corners off and turned in, a safety rotating down to the strong side
on nearly every early down (by the same nflverse count, Cover 3 on about 82 percent of their charted
first- and second-down dropbacks in 2019), and the same handful of rotations week after week. The 2021 Raiders are
the controlled experiment: a different roster, a new coordinator, and within one season their
coverage mix looks like the Chargers'.

**What to notice:** how *few* different pictures the defense shows. That is the Carroll philosophy,
and it has a modern cost: an offense that knows the coverage before the snap can call the concept
that beats it. In the same years, Vic Fangio's two-high defenses were showing quarterbacks a
different picture on every snap ([Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) tells
that story), and the league's split-safety rate climbed every year. The fact that Cover 3 was still
the most-charted single coverage in the NFL in 2025 says that the simple version keeps working;[^c3share]
the fact that it's now usually disguised says what changed. (The 2025 figure, about 28 percent,
comes from a different charting service than this chapter's 2018–2022 numbers, which label Cover 3
more often, so don't read the gap as a decline of ten points.)
:::

The coach who made it famous has moved on too. Carroll coached Seattle through the 2023 season and the
Raiders in 2025, when they went 3–14 and dismissed him after one year. Seattle won Super Bowl LX in
February 2026 under Mike Macdonald, with a split-safety defense from a different school (from Week
14 through the Super Bowl, two-high coverage on 54.8 percent of pass plays)
([Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)).[^carroll]
But nearly every NFL defense still plays Cover 3 on some early downs, usually as a match coverage,
usually arrived at by one of the three rotations above. The Seattle version didn't disappear; it
became part of everyone's playbook.

## Recognising Cover 3: before and after the snap

Everything above adds up to a two-step read you can make from your couch: a hypothesis before the
snap, a test one second after it. Here is the reasoning behind each check; the checklist at the end
of the section is the short version.

**Before the snap: the Cover 3 look.**

- **One safety deep in the middle**, 13 to 16 yards, roughly over the ball. *Why it matters:* the
  middle of the field is closed, which narrows the menu to the one-high coverages, Cover 3 and
  Cover 1.
- **Corners off and turned in**, 7 to 9 yards from their receivers with outside leverage, shoulders
  angled toward the quarterback. *Why:* a corner who must stay deeper than everyone in his third
  starts deep and watches the ball; a man corner is more often pressed and square to his receiver.
  Seattle-style corners who press and then carry are the exception, and you check them after the
  snap.
- **A safety down near the box**, 7 to 11 yards deep. *Why:* he is the fourth underneath defender
  and the eighth man against the run. Where he stands hints at the rotation: outside the slot or
  tight end suggests sky; inside, over the slot, with a nickel outside him, suggests buzz.
- **Underneath defenders in apex alignments**, a few yards inside the slot receivers, not tight on
  them. *Why:* zone defenders split the difference between a run fit and a pass drop; man defenders
  line up on their man.
- **The cloud tell**: a two-high look in which only *one* corner squats at 5 yards and the other is
  off, often with the free safety shaded toward the middle. *Why:* a real Cover 2 usually squats
  both corners; the off corner is already in a deep-third alignment. (Asymmetry is also how Cover 6
  looks, so check after the snap.)
- **Motion.** When a receiver motions across, watch the safeties. If they spin with him, one coming
  down on the new strong side and the other heading for the middle, the call is a single-high
  rotation tied to the strength; if a defender runs across with the motion man, think man coverage.

**After the snap: count the deep defenders, at one second.** About one second after the snap, look at
the deep part of the field and count the defenders backpedalling or running away from the line,
spread across the width. Three means a Cover 3 family call (Cover 3 or a three-deep fire zone); two
means Cover 2 or a relative; four means quarters; one means Cover 1 (with or without a robber, it's
still Cover 1). Two refinements make the count reliable:

- **Count early.** In Cover 3 match, the seam-flat defenders who carry slot receivers up the seams
  are 15 to 20 yards deep two seconds later and look like extra deep players (count the last panel
  of the match strip and you get five). The count means something only before the carries.
- **Check *who* the three are.** In Cover 3, two of them are the corners, deep and wide. If the
  corners are sitting in the flats and the middle man is a linebacker running down the middle of
  the field, it's [Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd), which also shows three deep at one
  second.

Then look underneath. Corners who keep their eyes inside and let a receiver who breaks short or
across go are zone; corners who turn and follow him across the field are man. A safety into the flat
is sky, a safety into the hook-curl is buzz, a corner sitting in the flat with a safety running over
him is cloud. Slot defenders who run away from a vertical release to a spot are spot-drop; slot
defenders who run with him up the seam are match. Four rushers and three deep is Cover 3; five
rushers and three deep, with a defensive lineman dropping into coverage, is a fire zone
([Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)).
And for how often a one-high picture before the snap is honest, and how to keep score of a defense
that lies, see [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: count to three"}
For one quarter, on every passing down:

- **Before the snap:** one high safety, corners off and turned in, a safety near the box? Say "Cover
  3" and guess sky (safety outside) or buzz (safety inside, nickel outside). Two-high with one
  squatting corner? Say "cloud?"
- **Motion:** do the safeties spin with it?
- **At one second, count deep defenders.** Three, with the corners among them, is the Cover 3
  family. Name the extra underneath player.
- **Watch one slot defender against a vertical release.** Away to a spot (spot-drop) or up the seam
  with him (match)?
- **Find the ball.** Hitch in front of a corner, seam between thirds, sail behind the curl-flat
  defender, or a check-down? On the replay, find the defender whose job that area was.
- **On early downs, count the box.** Eight near the line against a two-back or two-tight-end set,
  with one safety deep, is Cover 3's run defense. Watch for the play-action pass that punishes it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: Cover 3 in real tracking data"}
The NFL's Big Data Bowl files (no download is bundled with this book) label each play's coverage,
so you can find real Cover
3 plays and draw them with the same code. A sketch (the code is in the web version), assuming the
2025 edition's `plays.csv` and tracking files in `data/bdb/`:

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (finding a real Cover 3 play in Big Data Bowl data)"
from gridiron import bdb
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
c3 = plays[plays["pff_passCoverage"].str.startswith("Cover-3", na=False)]   # Cover-3, Cover-3 Seam, ...
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=c3["gameId"].iloc[0], play_id=c3["playId"].iloc[0])
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])          # count the deep defenders at +1.0 s
```

The coverage labels come from PFF's charting and split Cover 3 into variants whose names map onto
this chapter: labels such as `Cover-3 Seam` (Cover 3 with the seams carried, roughly the match
version) and `Cover-3 Cloud` left and right (the corner rotation), alongside plain `Cover-3`. Check
the year's data dictionary for the exact strings before filtering on them. The diagrams in this
chapter are simulated in the same format (`Play.to_tracking()`), which is why the two draw
identically.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: first-and-10, two tight ends"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sky
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10, ball in the middle, 12 personnel (two tight ends, Y and U, attached to the line; X and Z split wide). The defense is in its base 4-3: the Sam (Sm), Mike (M) and Will (W) linebackers behind four linemen. One safety (FS) is 15 yards deep in the middle; the strong safety (SS) is 8 yards deep, about 3 yards outside the right tight end; both corners (CB) are 8 yards off with outside leverage. The safeties are ringed; the orange line is the line to gain."
off12 = offense("ace")
d12 = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off12)
mv = {"SS": (8.0, 8.0), "FS": (15.0, 0.0), "LCB": (8.0, -16.2), "RCB": (8.0, 16.2)}
d12 = [q.moved(d=mv[q.key][0], w=mv[q.key][1], label="CB" if q.pos == "CB" else q.label)
       if q.key in mv else q for q in d12]
d12 = [q.moved(label="Sm") if q.key == "SAM" else q for q in d12]
pp1 = Play(off12, d12, los=LOS, to_go=10)
pp1.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = draw(pp1, lateral=(-23, 23), window=(-9.0, 19.0))
plt.show()
```

**What coverage family is this, what will the strong safety do at the snap, and if the offense
wants to throw, where should it aim?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Cover 3 (or its man cousin, Cover 1), with the strong safety rotating down: a sky look.** One
safety deep in the middle closes the middle of the field; the corners off and outside say zone, deep
thirds. The strong safety at 8 yards outside the tight end is the tell: he's the eighth man in the
box and the force player against a run to his side, and against a pass he'll come down and out to the
curl-flat area. The other three underneath jobs fall to the linebackers: the Sam takes the right
hook-curl, the Mike the left hook, and the Will widens to the left curl-flat. Against 12 personnel on
first down the defense is daring the offense to run into eight.

If the offense throws, the soft spots are the ones this chapter drew. **Play-action** first: the
safety and linebackers are reading run, so a fake handoff followed by a tight end up the seam, or a
deep crossing route behind the linebackers, attacks the exact space the eighth man left. Without a
fake, the **hitch** in front of the bailing corners and the **seam** away from the safety's lean are
there. The defense accepts all of that in exchange for a run defense with a spare man.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: two-high, but the corners don't match"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-cloud
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-7 against 11 personnel in a 2x2, ball in the middle. Two safeties deep: the free safety (FS) 13 yards deep, about 2 yards left of the ball, inside the left hash; the strong safety (SS) 12 yards deep, wide, between the right hash and the numbers. The right cornerback is squatting about 5 yards off Z with outside leverage; the left cornerback is 8 yards off X. The nickel ($) is in an apex over the left slot. Both corners and both safeties are ringed."
pp2 = Play(spread(), nickel({"MIKE": (4.5, 2.4), "WILL": (4.5, -2.2), "NB": (5.0, -7.0), "LCB": (8.0, -16.3),
                             "RCB": (5.0, 16.4), "FS": (13.0, -2.0), "SS": (12.0, 11.0)}), los=LOS, to_go=None)
pp2.highlight("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = draw(pp2, lateral=(-23, 23), window=(-7.5, 18.5))
plt.show()
```

**The shell says two-high. What else could it be, which corner gives it away, and what will you
check one second after the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Probably Cover 3 cloud to the right, with Cover 6 as the other possibility.** In a true Cover 2 both
corners usually squat in the flats; here only the right one does, and the left one is off at 8 yards
in a deep-third alignment. A squatting corner with a safety deep over him on one side and an off
corner on the other is the cloud picture: at the snap, the right corner plays the flat, the strong
safety runs to the deep right third behind him, and the free safety rotates to the middle. The free
safety's alignment helps: he's inside the hash, almost over the ball, while the strong safety is wide
over the squatting corner. Two Cover 2 safeties would be balanced, each on or outside his hash. A
safety cheated toward the middle is already halfway to the deep middle third.

The same pre-snap picture also fits **[Cover 6](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-6)**,
quarters on one half and Cover 2 on the other, which
[Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd) builds; its quarters side
also has a corner off the ball, so here it would be quarters on the left and Cover 2 on the right. **One second after the snap, look at the free safety.** If he
runs to the middle of the field, it's three deep: cloud. If he stays on the left and reads the slot
receiver, it's two deep: Cover 6. Either way, the right side looks the same, which is the point of
the disguise. Against cloud, the place to attack is the deep right third, where a safety has to run
with Z.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: two seconds after the snap"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-flood
#| fig-cap: "A Cover 3 sky play against a flood to the right, 2.2 seconds after the snap (simulated). Faint lines are where each player has been. Z is running a go route with the right cornerback over him; Y, from the slot, has pushed upfield and is breaking toward the sideline at about 12 yards (a sail route); the back (R) is running to the right flat. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is the curl-flat defender on that side; the Mike (M) has widened from his hook toward the curl. On the left, X and H run to hold the nickel ($), the Will and the free safety."
def flood_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), nickel(C3_PRE | {"SS": (6.5, 7.5)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    p.route("Z", [(-0.7, 15.0), (8.0, 15.8), (30.0, 17.0)], absolute=True)
    p.route("Y", [(-1.5, 9.0), (10.0, 9.8), (13.6, 15.2), (14.6, 20.5)], absolute=True)
    p.route("RB", [(-5.0, 1.5), (-3.4, 5.0), (1.6, 11.0), (3.0, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)
    p.route("X", [(-0.7, -15.0), (12.0, -15.6), (10.6, -14.6)], absolute=True)
    p.route("H", [(-1.5, -9.0), (6.0, -8.0), (26.0, -6.6)], absolute=True)
    p.drop("RCB", (24.0, 17.4), speed=6.2)
    p.drop("LCB", (18.0, -16.8), speed=5.0)
    p.drop("FS", (18.0, 0.4), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("SS", (9.8, 13.0), speed=4.4)
    p.drop("NB", (10.5, -11.8), speed=4.4)
    p.drop("WILL", (9.0, -4.4), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (9.5, 7.5), speed=4.0)
    return p

fp = flood_play()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
fld = moment(ax, fp, 2.25, (-24.5, 24.5), (-9.0, 26.0), rings=("SS",))
ruler(fld, fp)
plt.show()
```

**Who's the quarterback's read, what has that defender done, and where does the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The read is the strong safety, the curl-flat defender, and he has sunk under the sail route, so the
ball goes to the back in the flat.** This is the flood: three receivers at three depths on the right
(the go, the sail, the flat) against two defenders, the corner and the curl-flat defender. The corner
did his job, staying on top of Z's go route, which leaves the safety alone with two receivers. He's
at about 10 yards, wide, in the window where the sail will arrive, so the back, running to the flat
underneath him with nobody within 7 yards, is the throw. Had the safety jumped down toward the flat,
the sail behind him would have been open instead. (Notice the Mike in the frame, too: with #2 going outside and the back heading for the flat, he has widened from his hook toward the curl, as he's taught, and he still can't reach the flat in time.)

If this were Cover 3 match, the picture would differ only a little: with #2 (Y) releasing vertically
the safety would have carried him at first, and when Y broke out to the sail he'd stay with him, while
the Mike, who matches the back (#3), would have a long way to run to the flat. The flat would still be
the throw. Flood beats both versions for the same reason. There are only so
many defenders on one side of the field.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Cover 3 is three deep and four under.** The corners take the outside thirds and a safety the
  middle; two curl-flat defenders and two hook defenders take the underneath areas; four rush. It
  guards the whole deep field with only three players, which is why it's the NFL's most common zone.
- **Its bargain is the eighth man.** Bringing the second safety down gives the defense an extra run
  defender (and its force or alley player) while still playing three deep. The price is the seams,
  the soft spots in front of the corners, and an underneath defender with two zones.
- **Sky, buzz and cloud are three ways to arrive at the same coverage.** Sky sends a safety to the
  curl-flat, buzz sends him inside to the hook-curl while an outside defender takes the flat, and cloud
  puts the corner in the flat with a safety over him. Each fits a different player to the job and leaks
  a different pre-snap tell.
- **The curl-flat defender is the key, and the match version changed his job.** In spot-drop he guards
  a place and lets the seam go by; as a seam-flat defender in Cover 3 match he carries #2 up the seam
  first, which turns four verticals from an unsolvable count into four-on-four.
- **Seattle made it an identity.** Carroll's 2010s Seahawks showed one picture (a single high safety,
  pressed corners) and played Cover 3 or its man twin Cover 1 behind it, with a rangy free safety, a
  box strong safety and long corners who pressed and carried receivers into their thirds. They led
  the league in scoring defense four years running and sent coordinators across the league;
  Bradley's defenses still topped the Cover 3 charts years later.
- **Recognise it by counting.** One high safety, corners off and turned in, a safety near the box
  before the snap; three deep defenders one second after it, two of them the corners (count before
  the match carries, and don't mistake Tampa 2's running Mike for a third deep defender).

[^match]: Matty F. Brown, "Analysis: Kam Chancellor, Super Bowl XLVIII, and How Seahawks Play Cover 3," SI All Seahawks (May 30, 2021): https://www.si.com/nfl/seahawks/onsi/gm-report/analysis-kam-chancellor-super-bowl-xlviii-and-how-seahawks-play-cover-3 ("Seattle uses its high safety ... and leans him 60-40 in his middle deep 1/3 to one seam. The down safety ... matches the second seam route from his underneath zone"); Matty Brown, "Soft Sky: How Pete Carroll defends four verts from Middle of the Field Close," USA Football (Mar. 29, 2019): https://blogs.usafootball.com/blog/7141/soft-sky-how-pete-carroll-defends-four-verts-from-middle-of-the-field-close (the corners press in "read 1/3" technique and run with a vertical release). The precise rules changed by opponent and season; this is a summary of the common thread.
